query: AlCrFeNiSi belongs to a high-entropy-alloy family developed to combine properties that traditional single-principal-element alloys often cannot achieve simultaneously. Earlier research sought stable solid solutions and adjusted HEA compositions to target particular properties, but tradeoffs persisted: the CoCrFeMnNi system has limited wear and corrosion resistance, manganese can promote oxidation and oxide spallation, and cobalt-containing systems raise cost and processability concerns. Conventional bulk fabrication can cause compositional segregation during cooling, whereas mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing techniques can generate residual thermal stresses that impair mechanical performance and increase processing complexity. Given cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, what single intervention could improve mechanical integrity while limiting segregation, residual stress, and defect formation? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its causal mechanism, a quantitative or directional outcome relative to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, the processing and test boundaries of validity, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In situ substrate preheating during laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi powder reduces thermal gradients during solidification, thereby minimizing compositional segregation, residual stresses, and defect formation, which together improve mechanical integrity compared to conventional processing without preheating.
generation.material_initial_state: Cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock prepared for L-PBF additive manufacturing.
generation.intervention: Introduce an in situ substrate preheating step during the L-PBF process.
generation.conditions: Processing under standard L-PBF parameters in an inert atmosphere with all laser settings constant except for the preheated build platform. Mechanical tests and microstructural analyses are conducted at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced thermal gradients in the molten pool and surrounding material leading to a more uniform nucleation and finer grain structure.
generation.mechanism: Preheating the substrate lowers the temperature differential during processing, which slows the cooling rate and limits abrupt thermal shocks. This reduced undercooling minimizes the time available for solute diffusion and segregation and decreases residual tensile stresses, thereby reducing defect formation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples built with substrate preheating are expected to show lower levels of residual stress, reduced microstructural segregation, and fewer defects, resulting in improved mechanical properties (e.g., enhanced tensile strength and ductility) compared to conventionally processed builds.
generation.baseline: AlCrFeNiSi parts processed by L-PBF without substrate preheating, which typically exhibit significant segregation, higher residual stresses, and associated mechanical limitations.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is valid for L-PBF additive manufacturing of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi under controlled atmospheric conditions and standard laser parameters. Effects may vary with different preheat temperatures, alternative AM techniques, or other alloy systems.
generation.uncertainty: While improvements in mechanical integrity are anticipated, the exact magnitude of enhancement depends on the preheat temperature settings and specific processing conditions, and further investigation is needed to quantify the changes.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of AlCrFeNiSi specimens via L-PBF under identical conditions except that one set is produced with an elevated substrate temperature (selected based on pre-experimental optimization) and the other with a room temperature substrate. Ensure that all other parameters (laser power, scan speed, hatch spacing, etc.) are held constant.
measurements: Residual stress analysis using X-ray diffraction or comparable methods
Microstructural characterization via SEM with EDS mapping to assess grain size uniformity and chemical segregation
Mechanical testing including tensile and hardness measurements to evaluate strength and ductility
Non-destructive evaluation (e.g., CT scanning) to quantify defect density
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the preheated specimens do not demonstrate statistically significant reductions in residual stresses, lower compositional segregation, or improved mechanical properties relative to the control specimens, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThe CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy is commonly used for vascular stents due to its excellent mechanical support and ductility. However, as high-entropy alloy stents can cause inflammation in the blood vessels, leading to their re-narrowing, drug-eluting stents have been developed. These stents have nanopores on their surfaces that can carry drug particles to inhibit inflammation and effectively prevent re-narrowing of the blood vessels. To optimize the mechanical properties and drug-carrying capacity of high-entropy alloy stents, a high-entropy alloy system with different wide and deep square-shaped nanopore distributions is created using molecular dynamics. The mechanical characteristics and dislocation evolution mechanism of different nanopore high-entropy alloy systems under tensile stress were studied. The results showed that the CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy with a rational nanopore distribution can effectively maintain the mechanical support required for a vascular stent. This research provides a new direction for the manufacturing process of nanopores on the surfaces of high-entropy alloy stents.Keywords: mechanical properties, high-entropy alloy, drug-eluting stent,

Manufacturing processes have a strong influence on the mechanical properties of HEAs. It has been determined that the CoCrFeNi part produced by the hot-rolling process has a better yield and ultimate strength compared to the casted parts [,,,]. Additive manufacturing processes, such as Laser-Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF), can improve the mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys due to their inherent unique processing characteristics. Specifically, the rapid solidification and repeated remelting associated with these techniques facilitate the formation of fine grains and numerous substructures with a high density of dislocations, thereby enhancing the yield strength compared to conventionally processed alloys. Brif et al. [] showed that the yield strength of the CoCrFeNi alloy produced by the powder bed fusion (PBF) process is twice, respectively, the treble of that alloy in as-cast condition, and Kuzminova [] showed in turn that the yield strength of alloys using L-PBF is twice than that of hot-rolled alloys. However, the thermal cycling and partial remelting experienced by previous layers can significantly increase the hot cracking susceptibility of superalloys [].

drafts.hypothesis: Incorporating in situ substrate preheating during the additive manufacturing of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi powder can reduce thermal gradients, thereby limiting compositional segregation, residual stress, and defect formation while enhancing overall mechanical integrity.
drafts.intervention: Apply a controlled in situ substrate preheating (e.g., maintaining an elevated temperature during processing)
drafts.conditions: Additive manufacturing (such as laser powder bed fusion) performed in an atmosphere that minimizes oxidation, with preheating temperatures maintained consistently (for instance around 300–500°C) throughout the build process.
drafts.structural_mediator: A more homogeneous microstructure with refined grain structure and reduced thermal gradients
drafts.mechanism: Preheating the substrate diminishes the rate of cooling and lowers thermal gradients during processing. This reduced undercooling minimizes the driving force for rapid solute diffusion and segregation, and it alleviates thermal shock, thereby cutting down the formation of residual stresses and defects.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi (without preheating), the preheated builds are expected to exhibit lower residual stress, decreased microstructural segregation, fewer inherent defects (like porosity or cracking), and improved mechanical properties (enhanced strength and ductility).
drafts.baseline: Conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi produced via additive manufacturing at room temperature substrate conditions.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis applies to the processing of AlCrFeNiSi using additive manufacturing in environments where oxidation is controlled. Results might vary with different additive techniques, alternative heat management strategies, or other alloy compositions.

falsification_experiment.design: Process two sets of identical AlCrFeNiSi powder builds using an additive manufacturing system: one set under standard conditions (room temperature substrate) and the other using the specified in situ substrate preheating. Characterize both sets using residual stress measurements via X-ray diffraction, microstructural analysis with SEM and EDS mapping, mechanical testing (tensile and hardness tests), and non-destructive evaluation (such as computed tomography to assess defect density).
measurements: Residual stress levels via X-ray diffraction
Microstructure homogeneity and grain size via SEM/EDS
Defect density via computed tomography or similar methods
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the preheated samples show no significant reduction in residual stress, segregation, or defect formation and do not exhibit improved mechanical properties compared to standard builds, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: In situ substrate pre-heating during powder bed fusion additive manufacturing of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi reduces thermal gradients, which in turn minimizes compositional segregation, residual stresses, and defect formation, thereby improving mechanical integrity compared to conventionally processed parts.
drafts.intervention: Apply substrate pre-heating to the build platform during the laser-based powder bed fusion process.
drafts.conditions: Processing in an inert atmosphere with standard powder bed fusion parameters, where the build platform is maintained at an elevated temperature (e.g., within a range that approaches but does not exceed the alloy's solidification window).
drafts.mechanism: Pre-heating the substrate reduces the cooling rate and thermal gradient during deposition, allowing for more uniform alloying. This slower solidification minimizes local segregation of elements and decreases the buildup of residual tensile stresses, thereby limiting defect formation and enhancing the overall mechanical integrity.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Parts processed with pre-heated substrates will exhibit a finer, more uniform microstructure with reduced segregation, lower measured residual stresses, and improved mechanical properties (e.g., enhanced ductility and strength) relative to parts fabricated under conventionally cooled conditions.
drafts.baseline: Conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi parts using powder bed fusion without substrate pre-heating.
drafts.boundary: The validity of this hypothesis is limited to additive manufacturing of AlCrFeNiSi under controlled inert atmosphere conditions and within the accessible temperature ranges of current powder bed fusion systems. Extrapolation to bulk casting or other fabrication methods is not supported.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCrFeNiSi samples via powder bed fusion: one set with the build platform pre-heated to a target temperature within the specified range, and a control set without pre-heating. Maintain all other processing parameters (e.g., laser power, scanning speed, layer thickness) constant. After fabrication, conduct microstructural analysis (e.g., SEM, EDS) to assess segregation, measure residual stresses using X-ray diffraction or neutron diffraction, and perform mechanical tests (tensile and hardness tests) to evaluate mechanical integrity.
measurements: Microstructure uniformity and phase distribution (via SEM/EDS)
Residual stress profiles (via X-ray or neutron diffraction)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-heated samples do not show statistically significant improvements in microstructural uniformity (i.e., reduced segregation), lower residual stress levels, and enhanced mechanical properties compared to the control samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Preheating the build substrate during additive manufacturing of cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock will reduce thermal gradients during processing, thereby limiting compositional segregation, residual stress, and defect formation, which in turn improves the mechanical integrity of the fabricated alloy.
drafts.material_initial_state: Cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock prepared for additive manufacturing (e.g., Laser Powder Bed Fusion).
drafts.intervention: Introduce a substrate/build-platform preheating step (e.g., raising the temperature to an elevated value during processing) during the laser additive manufacturing process.
drafts.conditions: Process conducted under standard L-PBF conditions in an inert atmosphere; all laser parameters remain constant except for the addition of substrate preheating. Mechanical testing and microstructural analysis are performed at room temperature.
drafts.structural_mediator: Lower thermal gradients during rapid solidification lead to a more uniform nucleation and grain growth, reducing segregation and encouraging a finer, more homogeneous microstructure with fewer residual stresses.
drafts.mechanism: Preheating the substrate reduces the temperature differential between the molten pool and the surrounding material, which slows the cooling rate slightly and minimizes thermal shock. This limits the development of residual thermal stresses and suppresses rapid compositional segregation, thereby reducing microstructural defects.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Relative to conventionally processed (non-preheated) AlCrFeNiSi, samples processed with substrate preheating are expected to exhibit lower residual stress and reduced segregation, resulting in improved mechanical properties such as increased tensile strength and ductility. The precise quantitative improvement is uncertain and may depend on the exact preheat temperature.
drafts.baseline: AlCrFeNiSi processed by conventional bulk fabrication or standard L-PBF processing without substrate preheating, which typically shows significant compositional segregation and residual stresses.
drafts.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective for L-PBF-type additive manufacturing of high-entropy alloys where rapid solidification issues are pronounced. Its benefits might vary with different preheat temperatures, laser parameters, or if applied to fabrication techniques with inherently different thermal profiles.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of AlCrFeNiSi samples using L-PBF: one with the substrate preheated to a chosen elevated temperature (e.g., ~250°C) and a control set without preheating. All other processing parameters (laser power, scan speed, hatch spacing, etc.) must be identical.
measurements: Residual stress assessment (e.g., via X-ray diffraction or hole-drilling methods)
Microstructural characterization (using SEM/EDS to evaluate grain size uniformity and chemical segregation)
Mechanical testing (tensile strength, ductility, hardness measurements)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the preheated samples do not exhibit statistically significant reductions in residual stresses and segregation and do not show improved mechanical integrity compared with the control group, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: Implementing high-speed laser additive manufacturing for processing cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock will yield a more homogenous microstructure with reduced elemental segregation, lower residual stresses, and fewer defects, thereby enhancing its mechanical integrity compared to conventional bulk or low-speed processed samples.
drafts.material_initial_state: Cobalt‐free AlCrFeNiSi alloy powder that, when conventionally processed, tends to exhibit segregation, high residual thermal stresses, and defect formation.
drafts.intervention: Apply high-speed laser additive manufacturing (in particular, operating at an optimized high scanning speed during L-PBF) to process the powder feedstock.
drafts.conditions: This intervention is effective under controlled volumetric energy density conditions to ensure rapid solidification without inducing porosity; tests are conducted at room temperature with comparably prepared samples.
drafts.structural_mediator: A refined, uniform microstructure with reduced columnar grain size and minimal compositional gradients that mitigates segregation and defect nucleation.
drafts.mechanism: Increased scanning speeds enhance the cooling rate and reduce thermal gradients during solidification. This rapid solidification minimizes the time available for element partitioning and diffusion, thereby reducing segregation, limiting the development of residual stresses, and suppressing defect formation. The resulting microstructure supports improved dislocation interactions, enhancing mechanical strength and ductility.
drafts.predicted_outcome: Produced samples will exhibit higher yield strength and improved ductility with lower defect densities and more uniform phase distributions relative to those made by conventional or lower scanning speed processes.
drafts.baseline: Conventional processing methods or low scanning speed laser additive manufacturing, which typically lead to greater segregation, higher residual stresses, and more internal defects in AlCrFeNiSi alloys.
drafts.boundary: The hypothesis applies to AlCrFeNiSi powders processed via laser-based additive manufacturing under optimized energy density conditions; results may differ if the energy input or other process parameters vary significantly or when applied to different alloy compositions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCrFeNiSi specimens using L-PBF: one at an optimized high scanning speed (ensuring high volumetric energy density with rapid solidification) and one at a conventional lower scanning speed. Characterize both sets for microstructural uniformity (grain size, phase distribution, elemental segregation) using SEM, EDS, and XRD. Perform standardized mechanical testing (tensile tests, hardness measurements) to compare yield strength, ductility, and defect density.
measurements: Grain size distribution and elemental mapping (via SEM/EDS)
Phase identification and residual stress analysis (via XRD)
Mechanical properties including yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, elongation, and hardness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high scanning speed samples do not show statistically significant improvements in mechanical properties (e.g., yield strength, ductility) and microstructural uniformity (e.g., reduced segregation and defects) relative to the low scanning speed samples—or if adverse effects such as increased porosity or cracking are observed—the hypothesis will be falsified.
